title: Cap. VIII: Ex vs.16 — κρίμα opposed to δώρημα; Garissoles syllogism
pass_a_gloss: Garissoles's third argument starts from Romans 5:16. He says the Apostle sets Adam's κρίμα (the judgment or the guilt-verdict that comes from Adam) over against Christ's δώρημα. From that opposition he infers: δώρημα does not name a quality that lives in us; it names what stands in Christ and is freely counted to us in Christ. Therefore κρίμα likewise must name something outside us — the very fault Adam committed — and from that outside fault we pull guilt and condemnation. The collected syllogism: whatever fault runs out into the condemnation of all must be imputed to all; Adam's fault does so run; therefore Adam's fault must be imputed to all.
pass_b_english: III. From verse 16 he reasons thus. Here κρίμα, judgment or guilt from Adam, is set opposite Christ's δώρημα (Romans 5:16). Therefore, as δώρημα does not signify some quality inhering in us, but what is in Christ, and is freely imputed to us in Christ, so κρίμα must signify something outside us — namely the fault committed by Adam, from which we draw guilt and condemnation. Collect: Whose fault is unto the condemnation of all, that fault must be imputed to all. But Adam's fault is unto the condemnation of all. Therefore it must be imputed to all.
source_text: III. Ex verf. 16. sic ratiocinatur. Hic κρίμα, judicium sive reatus ex Adamo, opponitur δώρημα Christi. Ergo ut δώρημα non significat qualitatem aliquam nobis inherentem, sed quod in Christo est, & in Christo nobis gratis imputatur; Ita κρίμα aliquid significare debet, quod sit extra nos, nempe culpam ab Adamo patratam, unde reatum & condemnationem trahimus. Collige. Cujus culpa est in omnium condemnationem, eam omnibus imputari oportet. Atqui culpa Adami est in omnium condemnationem. Ergo eam omnibus imputari oportet.
